caveats: Primary groove class comes from audio usage (drums, hats, snare, bass, tempo), never from playlist or title.
History, culture, and psychology are encyclopedia knowledge attached to that class and then instantiated with this file's BPM, key, and percussion usage.
Western major/minor valence findings do not universalize; they are cited as listener-research tendencies, not laws.
Related genres are a well-rounded map of the tradition, not a claim that this file is those genres.
Psychoacoustics here is a listening-study model (entrainment, groove, tactile bass), not a medical or therapeutic claim.

science.entrainment: Sensorimotor synchronization (Large & Snyder; Repp) explains why a stable pulse recruits movement. Club musics around 118–128 BPM sit near preferred tapping rates and walking cadence, which is why four-on-the-floor feels bodily rather than merely metric.
science.syncopation: Witek et al. showed moderate syncopation maximizes groove pleasure; too little feels stiff, too much feels broken. Offbeat hats and bass-off-the-kick are the house/disco case of that curve.
science.halfTime: A snare on beat 3 at a high clock BPM is perceived closer to half that tempo (London, Hearing in Time). 152 with snare on 3 is a ~76 dub/dancehall pocket, not a 152 trance ride, unless hats are used as a 16th wash.
science.subBass: Energy below ~60 Hz is felt as vibration (vestibular/tactile) as well as heard. Sound-system culture (Jamaica, UK) and 808 music exploit that channel. A spectral 'sub' label is not automatically trap; house and disco also sit on sub.
science.modeValence: In many Western listeners, major modes trend toward higher valence and minor toward lower (Juslin, Gabrielsson). This is a statistical tendency, not a universal code — modal, pentatonic, and non-Western practices do not obey the same map.
science.delaySpace: Dub mixing (King Tubby, Lee Perry) treats delay and spring reverb as compositional instruments. Spatially repeating snare/hat is a psychological 'hallucinated architecture' — the room becomes a second drummer.
science.sidechain: House/techno pumping is amplitude modulation locked to kick, a learned club cue for 'the floor is breathing' rather than a genre by itself.
science.socialCoupling: Shared pulse is a social technology: people use it to align movement, talk in the gaps, and feel 'in the room together' (Phillips-Silver & Keller on joint action; Clayton on entrainment in ensemble). Offbeat hats invite filling space with the body; sparse hats invite huddling around bass.
science.activationFormula: The musical DNA formula for a listener is ordered, not a mood adjective: (1) drum grid sets the body map, (2) tempo/feel sets arousal window, (3) bass lock tells the hips whether to bounce, skank, or hover, (4) hats/snare/instruments are the social cue (ride vs space), (5) spectrum and key color valence. Effects are tendencies in hearing and movement, not guaranteed inner states.

Funky House.history: House is disco's afterlife after the 1979 'Disco Sucks' backlash and the warehouse continuum in Chicago (Knuckles at the Warehouse) and New York (Levan at the Garage). Funky / disco house keeps the offbeat hi-hat and syncopated bass of disco rather than techno's kick-locked ostinato. Nu-disco and French house later re-sampled that language with compression and filters. The science of the style is groove: kick as heartbeat, hats as lift, bass as conversation with the kick.
Funky House.culture: House floors were historically Black, Latino, and queer sanctuary spaces. The offbeat hat is a social cue — it invites the body to fill the space between kicks. Cross-cultural traffic includes disco strings, gospel piano, Afro-Cuban percussion, and later UK garage shuffle.
Funky House.psychology: Predictable 4/4 plus moderate syncopation supports trance-like motor coupling without the dissociative density of 16th-hat trance. Warm minor/major soul harmony plus swing reads as affiliation and play rather than aggression. Listeners often report 'lift' on the offbeat hat — a small prediction error that resolves every beat.
Funky House.theory: Meter is almost always 4/4. Harmony is often diatonic or modal (Dorian/Aeolian) with loop-based rather than sonata form: 8/16-bar cells, breakdown/build as tension architecture. Bass typically emphasizes upbeats or syncopated 8ths against downbeat kicks.
Funky House.production: Analog-leaning drum machines (909/707 hats, 808/acoustic kick), sidechained bass, relatively open midrange for keys/guitar chops. Swing quantization (often 16th swing 20–50%) is a style marker.

Tech House.history: Tech house names the overlap of house groove and techno's reduced palette. UK rooms in the late 1990s used it as a functional peak-time language: still 4/4 and still for dancing, but drier, more percussive, less disco orchestra. It is a club technology more than a nationalist style.
Tech House.culture: Warehouse and after-hours culture: endurance, darkness, repetition as social contract. Less gospel-house communion, more machinic intimacy.
Tech House.psychology: High repetition + sparse harmonic change induces a flow state (Csikszentmihalyi's challenge/skill balance for dancing). Rolling hats raise temporal density without changing the downbeat map, which increases arousal while preserving orientation.
Tech House.theory: Loop form; often minor modes; bass may roll in 8ths or lock nearer the kick than funky house. Percussion layers create implied polyrhythm against a stable grid.
Tech House.production: Short decays, controlled sub, mid percussion transients, fewer pad beds than melodic house.

Deep House.history: Deep house named a more inward, chord-rich house — Heard's 'Can You Feel It' as a canonical emotional template. Later commercial 'deep house' (2010s radio) often meant tropical vocals at 120; the original sense is harmonic depth and patience.
Deep House.culture: Loft and after-hours listening-dancing: intimacy over spectacle.
Deep House.psychology: Slower harmonic rhythm and softer transients lower defensive arousal while the 4/4 still affords movement — a regulated, affiliative state.
Deep House.theory: Extended tertian harmony (9ths, 11ths), often minor with major-7 color; 4/4 with notable swing.
Deep House.production: Warm analog bass, rhodes/pads, less aggressive limiting than peak-time house.

House.history: The parent language of electronic dance music's 4/4 club practice. Acid house (303) is a sibling branch; this class is the generic 118–128 pulse when usage is house but not further specified.
House.culture: Dance floor as temporary autonomous zone — historically marginalized communities first.
House.psychology: Isochronous pulse + backbeat is the most widely shared motor template in global pop/club music.

techniques: 4/4 just under or at house tempo
Disco.history: Disco synthesized soul, funk, Latin percussion, and European production into a 4/4 social music. The 1979 backlash pushed the culture underground, where it became house. Nu-disco is the 21st-century electronic restatement.
Disco.culture: Queer, Black, and immigrant club cultures; fashion and spectacle as political presence.
Disco.psychology: Slightly slower than peak house can feel more 'body-roll' than 'stomp'. Offbeat hats create the classic disco bounce.
Disco.theory: 4/4, often major or mixolydian brightness; bass ostinatos; 16-bar verse structures inherited from song form.
Disco.production: Open hats, live or live-feel bass, wider stereo than dry techno.

influences: Juan Atkins / Derrick May / Kevin Saunderson
Techno.history: Detroit techno framed itself as Afro-futurist machine soul, not as 'soulless' European functionalism — though Berlin later became the civic capital of the 4/4 night. Peak-time techno is the high-density club dialect.
Techno.culture: Post-industrial cities, all-night permission structures, sound as architecture.
Techno.psychology: High temporal density and low lyrical content favor absorption and reduced self-talk — a sought dissociative-but-safe state on a predictable grid.
Techno.theory: 4/4 above typical house pocket; functional harmony often static; timbre and arrangement carry form.
Techno.production: Hard kick, controlled low mids, hats as pressure.

Reggae.history: Reggae and dub are among the most influential production cultures of the 20th century. One-drop withholds the kick on beat 1; steppers restores a marching 4/4 under still-heavy bass. Dub invented remix culture: the mix as composition, delay as instrument. UK steppers and digital dancehall (Sleng Teng, 1985) electrified the grid. A 140–152 clock with snare on 3 is the doubled reading of a ~70–76 skank — the same pocket as much dancehall and dub, not trance.
Reggae.culture: Rastafari, sound-system democracy, migrant Britain, bass as social weight. The 'space' in the drum kit is political: room for the voice of bass and for the crowd.
Reggae.psychology: Sub-bass plus half-time snare slows perceived locomotion and can induce a grounded, almost trance-meditative motor pattern distinct from house's bounce. Dub delay creates expectation and echoic memory loops — a mild, pleasurable prediction game.
Reggae.theory: Often minor/pentatonic bass riffs; harmonic rhythm slow; emphasis on beats 2 and 4 or beat 3 depending on one-drop vs rockers/steppers. Clock BPM may be notated doubled.
Reggae.production: Heavy sub, spring/plate/tape delay, dropout, keyed FX. Hats used as space or skank, not as a 16th club wash.

Trap.history: Trap named a Southern hip-hop locale and then a global drum dialect: half-time snare, stutter hats, 808 as bass and kick. It is not 'any 140 BPM'. Without 16th hat language it often reads as dub, dancehall, or bass music instead.
Trap.culture: Street reportage, hustle narratives, then fashion/internet aesthetics. The 808 is a Black American electronic instrument history (hip-hop, Miami bass, Detroit) as much as a plugin preset.
Trap.psychology: Half-time snare at 140 creates a slow swagger over a fast hat clock — dual-timescale arousal (London). Hat rolls are startle/ornament, raising phasic attention.
Trap.theory: Often minor pentatonic 808; sparse harmony; 16-bar loops; hi-hat as the fast stratum of a stratified meter.
Trap.production: Tuned 808 with glide, hard clip/saturation, wide stereo hats, dry punchy snare.

Hip-Hop.history: Hip-hop's drum language comes from funk breaks and Jamaican sound-system culture in the Bronx. Boom-bap is a snare-on-2-and-4 school; trap is a later Southern half-time school. Broken beat without 808 dominance still sits in this family.
Hip-Hop.culture: MC/DJ/graffiti/dance as a four-element culture; sampling as archival politics.
Hip-Hop.psychology: Head-nod groove (70–95 or half-time 140) favors nodding and lyric encoding over continuous club stomp.
Hip-Hop.theory: Often 4/4 with swung 16ths; sampled harmony; backbeat primacy.
Hip-Hop.production: Sample grain, parallel compression, pocket quantization (Dilla-late vs tight).

Experimental Bass.history: After dubstep's 2011 pop peak, 'bass music' splintered into halftime, UK bass, experimental club. Broken drums plus sub without a house hat ride is that diaspora — not funky house even at 120–130. Footwork (Chicago) is a cousin: 160-ish with sliced kicks; wonky is off-grid 808.
Experimental Bass.culture: Internet-era scenes, pirate-radio UK, Black Atlantic bass as continuum (Gilroy) rather than isolated genres.
Experimental Bass.psychology: Unstable kick maps raise prediction error (groove as problem-solving). Sub still affords bodily coupling, so the state is alert rather than lost.
Experimental Bass.theory: Polymetric or syncopated kick; 808 pitch as melody; form often drop-based rather than 8-bar house.
Experimental Bass.production: Designed bass (FM, wavetable, resample), transient kicks, negative space.

Drum & Bass.history: Jungle/DnB accelerated hip-hop breaks and reggae bass into 160–180 BPM. Liquid keeps harmonic warmth; jungle keeps ragga and chopped-break chaos.
Drum & Bass.culture: UK rave, Black British identity, soundsystem bass as inheritance.
Drum & Bass.psychology: Very high event density; dual meter (drums fast, bass slow) is a hallmark of stratified attention.
Drum & Bass.theory: Breakbeat at high tempo; bass often half-time relative to drums.
Drum & Bass.production: Sliced breaks, Reese bass, amen editing.

Breaks.history: Breaks keep the funk-break DNA at club energy without jungle's 170 or trap's 808 dialect.
Breaks.culture: Rave-funk crossover, less soundsystem-sub than bass music.
Breaks.psychology: Syncopation-forward groove; more startle than house, more kick variety than techno.
Breaks.theory: Broken 4/4; snare often not a simple 2-and-4.

Dubstep.history: Early dubstep was garage's half-time, dub's space, and pirate-radio bass — not the later festival 'wub' caricature. 140 half-time is shared with trap; the difference is drum usage and bass design vs 16th hats.
Dubstep.culture: UK immigrant and working-class club nights; darkness as aesthetic.
Dubstep.psychology: Long gaps between snares increase anticipatory tension; sub drop is a startle-reward.
Dubstep.production: Sub-focused mastering, sparse mids, designed bass.

Reggaeton.history: The dembow riddim (from dancehall) is the metric DNA. Panamanian reggae en español and Puerto Rican underground made it a hemispheric pop engine.
Reggaeton.culture: Caribbean-Latin urban modernity; often gendered dance codes; global streaming-era lingua franca.
Reggaeton.psychology: The 3+3+2 grouping is highly dance-efficient (similar to countless Afro-Latin timelines) — body knows it before theory names it.
Reggaeton.theory: Dembow clave-like grouping over 4/4; typically 80–100 or doubled 160–180 notation.
Reggaeton.production: Dry snare, 808 or acoustic-hybrid kick, vocal forward.

Trance.history: Trance used 4/4 and busy cymbals plus harmonic yearning (suspended chords, long builds). It is not 'any fast 4/4': without a hat wash and mid harmonic bed, fast 4/4 is more likely techno, bass, or doubled dub.
Trance.culture: Rave spirituality, Goa backpacker ritual, superclub spectacle — different subcultures under one tempo band.
Trance.psychology: Continuous 8th/16th hats + slow harmonic builds favor oceanic self-transcendence reports (similar to repetitious ritual music). High BPM + busy ride raises arousal; pads provide a 'sky' for that energy.
Trance.theory: 4/4 132–150+; minor with progressive chord cycles; snare often 2-and-4 not half-time.
Trance.production: Wide supersaws/pads, long tails, relentless hats.

Hard Dance.history: Hard dance sits above trance tempo with harsher kick language.
Hard Dance.psychology: Very high arousal; kick as impact ritual.

Downtempo.history: Downtempo is club music's recovery room and hip-hop's unhurried cousin.
Downtempo.psychology: Below preferred dance cadence; parasympathetic-leaning if textures are soft.

Lo-Fi.history: A streaming-era reduction of boom-bap and jazz-hop into continuous texture.
Lo-Fi.psychology: Low-arousal backgrounding; reduced high-frequency energy lowers vigilance.

Minimal.history: Reduction as drama — fewer events, more noticing.
Minimal.psychology: Low event density increases sensitivity to tiny changes (predictive coding).
Minimal.production: Clicky percussion, deep but not busy bass.

Slow House.history: House pulse at a walking-slower cadence — still 4/4, not dub unless hats/sub usage says so.
Slow House.psychology: Lower BPM reduces motor urgency while keeping dance affordance.

Psychedelic House.history: Psychedelic house keeps the house 4/4 as a body map and puts the trip in the midrange and FX: acid 303 language, modal drones from psych rock, and dub delay as a second drummer. The floor still dances; the room becomes the hallucinated architecture.
Psychedelic House.culture: After-hours tents, sound-system sessions, and long-blend DJ culture — music as environment rather than peak-time stomp.
Psychedelic House.psychology: Stable kick plus slow-moving filters and long tails create motor coupling with mild prediction-error haze — the float-while-dancing state. Delay repeats turn space into rhythm.
Psychedelic House.theory: 4/4 loop form, often Dorian or Mixolydian; long 16/32-bar cells; delayed percussion as counter-rhythm against the grid.
Psychedelic House.production: Analog synths, tape or spring delay, phaser, spacious reverb, less aggressive limiting than peak-time house.

Unclassified.history: Insufficient drum-grid or tempo evidence to attach a tradition with integrity.
Unclassified.psychology: Without a stable meter, motor coupling is weak; analysis stays at spectral description.
